title: JESUS CALLED IT ADULTERY… EVEN WHEN NOBODY TOUCHED ANYONE. WHY?
paragraphs: JESUS CALLED IT ADULTERY… EVEN WHEN NOBODY TOUCHED ANYONE. WHY?
The Terrifying Truth About Lust, the Secrets We Protect, and the Savior Who Sees What Nobody Else Can — What Matthew 5:27–30 Really Confronts
Nobody saw you.
Nobody heard what you were thinking.
Nobody knows what you searched for, what you imagined, what you kept looking at, or what happened inside your mind when someone walked past you.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your friends at church don't know.
And perhaps that is exactly why you have convinced yourself that nothing serious happened.
After all, you didn't touch anyone.
You didn't have an affair.
You didn't break your marriage vows physically.
You just looked.
You just imagined.
You just entertained a thought.
So why did Jesus Christ say something so shocking that, nearly two thousand years later, it still has the power to expose the most carefully guarded corners of the human heart?
Because Jesus was confronting something far deeper than what our hands do. He was confronting what our hearts have learned to desire.
And before you finish reading, you may discover that the most dangerous thing about secret sin is not simply that nobody else knows.
It is that you can become so comfortable hiding it that you forget you were never hidden from God.
But there is something else you need to hear.
Something that changes this entire conversation.
The same Jesus who exposes the hidden heart is the Savior who came to redeem it.

And if you have ever struggled with lust, pornography, secret fantasies, sexual temptation, betrayal, shame, or the exhausting cycle of promising God that you will never do it again, please don't leave before you understand what He was actually saying.
Because Matthew 5 is not merely a warning about what can destroy you.
It is also an invitation to the only One who can make you new.
Jesus was standing before people who knew the commandment.
They had heard it since childhood.
"You shall not commit adultery."
It was the seventh commandment, recorded in Exodus 20:14.
Straightforward.
Unmistakable.
And for many, perhaps reassuring.
They could examine their outward behavior and conclude that they had obeyed.
No physical affair.
No forbidden sexual encounter.
No visible violation.
Case closed.
Then Jesus spoke.
And suddenly, the courtroom moved from the outside of their lives into the secret chambers of their hearts.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus declares:
"You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart."
That wording follows the English Standard Version.
Now consider the original Greek of Matthew 5:28:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
A close rendering is:
"But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart."
Read that carefully.
Jesus was not merely describing the involuntary experience of noticing that another person is physically attractive.
He was confronting a deliberate direction of desire.
The Greek expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) communicates looking with a view toward desiring or coveting her.

The verb ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō) means to desire, long for, or covet. The word itself is not automatically sinful in every biblical context. Its moral meaning depends on what is desired and how that desire is directed.
But here, in the context of adultery, Jesus is confronting sexual desire that violates the rightful boundaries of love and faithfulness.
This is important.
Because there is a difference between recognizing beauty and deliberately feeding lust.
There is a difference between temptation arriving and the heart welcoming it as an honored guest.
There is a difference between an unwanted thought entering your mind and choosing to nurture that thought until another human being becomes an object of private sexual gratification.
Jesus was not declaring that every passing attraction is adultery.
He was exposing the kind of gaze that intentionally cultivates forbidden desire.
And that distinction matters enormously, especially to believers who already struggle with shame, anxiety, or intrusive thoughts.
Being tempted is not the same as choosing to sin.
Hebrews 4:15 teaches that Jesus Himself was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
Temptation alone cannot therefore be equated with moral failure.
But temptation can become an invitation.
And the question is what we do when it knocks.
Do we turn away?
Or do we open the door, pull up a chair, and ask it to stay?
That is where the confrontation becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have learned how to look innocent while secretly cultivating desires we would be ashamed to reveal.
We know how to close a browser when someone enters the room.
We know how to delete a conversation.
We know how to erase a search history.
We know how to explain away a flirtation.
We know how to call it harmless entertainment.
We know how to say, "It's just a fantasy."
But Jesus does not measure faithfulness only by whether another person can prove that something happened.
He sees the heart.
And sometimes the heart has already begun rehearsing a betrayal that the body has not yet committed.
That does not mean inward lust and physical adultery are identical in every consequence.
They are not.
Physical adultery involves additional acts of betrayal and harm that must never be minimized.
Jesus is not erasing those distinctions.
He is destroying the illusion that outward restraint automatically means inward purity.
A person can avoid an affair and still nurture an adulterous heart.
A person can appear faithful in public while secretly feeding desires that undermine faithfulness.
And a person can obey the letter of a commandment while resisting the love and holiness toward which that commandment points.
This is why Matthew 5 must be understood within the larger Sermon on the Mount.
Jesus was not casually inventing a new standard to make everyone feel guilty.
He was revealing the depth of God's righteous intention.
Just a few verses earlier, in Matthew 5:21–22, He confronted anger in connection with the commandment against murder.
His point was not that every angry thought carries the same earthly consequences as homicide.
His point was that righteousness cannot be reduced to avoiding the final outward act.
Sin often has roots long before it produces visible fruit.
And Jesus came to confront the roots.
Think about how quietly those roots can grow.
A marriage begins with affection.
Two people make promises.
They build a home.
They share responsibilities.
They raise children.
They pray together.
But somewhere along the way, emotional distance grows.
Conversations become shorter.
Affection becomes less frequent.
Disappointment accumulates.
And then someone else notices you.
A coworker laughs at your jokes.
An old acquaintance sends a message.
A stranger online gives you the attention you have been missing.
At first, it seems innocent.
You tell yourself there is nothing wrong with enjoying a little attention.
But then you begin looking forward to the messages.
You start sharing things you no longer share with your spouse.
You imagine what life might be like with that person.
You begin comparing.
You begin concealing.
And one day you realize that although you have never physically crossed the line, your heart has been walking toward it for months.
That is the kind of danger Jesus refuses to leave unnamed.
Not because He hates human desire.
But because He knows what happens when desire becomes detached from love, truth, covenant faithfulness, and obedience to God.
And perhaps your struggle does not involve another person in your life.
Perhaps it happens at midnight.
The house is quiet.
Everyone is asleep.
Your phone is glowing.
You tell yourself you are only going to scroll for a few minutes.
Then an image appears.
You stop.
You look again.
You know where this can lead.
You have been here before.
And somewhere inside you, there is a small, uncomfortable awareness that you are standing at a familiar crossroads.
You can turn away.
Or you can keep going.
Sometimes you turn away.
Sometimes you don't.
And afterward comes the silence.
The shame.
The familiar promise.
"Lord, this is the last time."
You mean it.
At least in that moment.
But days later, the same battle returns.
And eventually, the most frightening part is not simply the temptation.
It is the possibility that you will stop resisting.
That you will become numb.
That what once convicted you will eventually entertain you.
That you will learn to live two lives and call the arrangement normal.
Listen carefully.
The goal of Jesus' warning is not to convince you that you are beyond redemption. It is to awaken you before sin becomes something you no longer want to surrender.
There is another biblical connection here that makes His words even more profound.
Long before Jesus delivered the Sermon on the Mount, God gave Israel the tenth commandment.
In Exodus 20:17, the Hebrew text begins:
לֹא תַחְמֹד
Lo tachmod.
"You shall not covet."
The Hebrew verb חָמַד (chamad) can mean to desire, take pleasure in, or covet, depending on context.
The commandment specifically prohibits coveting what belongs to one's neighbor, including the neighbor's wife.
Notice what this reveals.
God's concern with inward desire was not a sudden invention in Matthew 5.
The law already addressed the human heart.
And when the Hebrew Scriptures were translated into Greek in the Septuagint, the commandment against coveting used a form of ἐπιθυμέω, the same verb family found in Jesus' teaching about lust.
That connection helps illuminate the seriousness of His words.
Jesus was not condemning the existence of every desire.
He was confronting desire that crosses the boundaries of what is righteous.
Desire that treats another person as something to possess.
Desire that refuses to respect the dignity of someone made in God's image.
Desire that says, "I want this," while pushing aside the question, "Does this honor God?"
And here is something our generation desperately needs to remember.
The person on the screen is a human being.
The person walking past you is a human being.
The person whose photograph you keep revisiting is a human being.
Not merely a body.
Not a collection of features.
Not an object created to satisfy your imagination.
A human being with dignity that does not depend on your desires.
Someone made in the image of God.
When lust takes control, it can train us to look at people primarily through the question of what they can provide for us.
But Christ calls us to a radically different way of seeing.
To recognize people as neighbors to love rather than objects to consume.
To see dignity where the world encourages exploitation.
To practice self-control where the culture celebrates indulgence.
To remember that love does not simply ask what it can take.
Love considers what it owes another person.
Respect.
Truth.
Faithfulness.
Honor.
And sometimes, the most loving thing you can do is turn your eyes away.
Not because the other person is shameful.
But because the other person is worthy of being treated as more than the object of your appetite.
Now we arrive at one of the most disturbing parts of Matthew 5.
Because Jesus did not stop after describing adultery of the heart.
He continued:
"If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away."
Then He spoke similarly about the right hand.
Matthew 5:29–30.
Those words are severe.
And they were meant to be.
But we must understand them correctly.
Jesus was using deliberately shocking, forceful imagery to communicate the seriousness of dealing with sin.
He was not commanding literal self-mutilation.
Removing a physical eye cannot remove sinful desire from the human heart.
And throughout Scripture, the problem of sin is consistently traced deeper than bodily anatomy.
Jesus Himself teaches in Mark 7:21–23 that evil thoughts and sinful actions proceed from within the human heart.
The point of Matthew 5:29–30 is therefore not physical injury.
It is decisive repentance.
Jesus is telling us not to negotiate endlessly with the very things that are leading us into sin.
Sometimes repentance means ending a private conversation.
Sometimes it means deleting an account.
Sometimes it means installing safeguards on your devices.
Sometimes it means refusing to revisit a website.
Sometimes it means confessing to a trustworthy, mature Christian who can help you pursue accountability.
Sometimes it means seeking qualified counseling when compulsive behavior, trauma, or deeply entrenched patterns are involved.
Sometimes it means admitting that the friendship you keep defending has crossed emotional boundaries you would not want your spouse to cross.
And sometimes it means surrendering something you genuinely enjoy because you recognize what it is doing to your soul.
Not everything that is permissible is beneficial.
Not everything that entertains you strengthens you.
Not everything you can access deserves access to you.
And not everything you have become accustomed to should be allowed to remain.
This is where many of us want a softer Jesus.
A Jesus who comforts us without confronting us.
A Jesus who forgives us without calling us to repentance.
A Jesus who understands our weakness but never asks us to change.
But that is not the Jesus revealed in Scripture.
The real Jesus is full of grace and truth.
He does not minimize sin.
He does not excuse exploitation.
He does not celebrate unfaithfulness.
He does not call darkness light.
And yet, astonishingly, He does not turn away from sinners who come to Him.
That is where this story becomes something more than a warning.
Because if Matthew 5 only told us what was wrong with our hearts, it would leave us exposed and desperate.
But the Gospel tells us what God has done for hearts like ours.
Consider the woman in John 8.
She was brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery.
Her accusers wanted judgment.
They stood ready to use her shame as a weapon.
And Jesus refused to join their hypocrisy.
One by one, the accusers departed.
Then Jesus addressed the woman.
He did not tell her that adultery was harmless.
He did not pretend sin did not matter.
But neither did He hand her over to the condemnation her accusers were demanding.
In John 8:11, He told her:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."

This account, traditionally known as the woman caught in adultery, is found in John 7:53–8:11. A careful reader should know that the passage is absent from the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John and is marked as textually disputed in many modern Bibles. Its themes of mercy and repentance, however, are also clearly taught in undisputed passages throughout the New Testament.
And those themes matter here.
Grace does not mean that sin is imaginary.
Grace means that sinners are not beyond the reach of Christ.
Forgiveness is not permission to continue destroying ourselves.
Forgiveness opens the door to a new life.
Jesus does not simply say, "I know what you did."
He calls us to come to Him, repent, believe, and follow.
And that invitation is not reserved for people whose sins are publicly acceptable.
It is for the person battling pornography.
The husband who has secretly entertained another woman.
The wife who has allowed an emotional attachment to grow beyond faithful boundaries.
The unmarried believer struggling with sexual fantasies.
The person who has crossed lines and now lives with regret.
The person whose sexual history has become a source of overwhelming shame.
The person who has confessed the same sin so many times that another prayer feels almost dishonest.
And the person who has become convinced that God must be tired of hearing their voice.
Perhaps that last person is you.
Perhaps you still attend church.
You still sing.
You still listen to sermons.
You still post Bible verses.
But somewhere beneath the surface, you carry a private accusation.
"If they knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way."
And perhaps you have begun imagining that Jesus feels the same.
But listen to what the apostle John writes in 1 John 1:9:
Notice the promise.
Not merely to forgive.
But to cleanse.
The Greek word translated "cleanse" is καθαρίσῃ (katharisē), from καθαρίζω (katharizō), meaning to cleanse or purify.
John is not offering a religious excuse for continuing in darkness.
The surrounding verses call believers to walk in the light.
But he is declaring something extraordinary about the mercy of God.
Sin does not have to remain the final word over a repentant person's life.
Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
His mercy is real.
And His call to holiness is inseparable from His gift of grace.
That does not mean the consequences of our choices instantly disappear.
Broken trust may require years of patient rebuilding.
A betrayed spouse may need safety, truth, time, and wise support.
Someone trapped in destructive habits may need sustained accountability and practical help.
Repentance does not demand that wounded people pretend nothing happened.
Nor does forgiveness eliminate the responsibility to make amends where possible.
But the Gospel does mean that your past does not have to be the master of your future.
And your struggle does not have to become your identity.
There is a beautiful connection in Matthew 5 that many readers overlook.
Before Jesus speaks about lust, He says:
"Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."
Matthew 5:8.
The Greek phrase is:
μακάριοι οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ
Makarioi hoi katharoi tē kardia.
"Blessed are the pure in heart."
The word καθαροί (katharoi) means pure or clean.
And καρδίᾳ (kardia) refers to the heart, the inward center of human thought, desire, and intention.
Jesus is not merely calling His disciples to manage appearances.
He is calling them to an inward life shaped by devotion to God.
Not simply clean hands in public.
But a heart increasingly surrendered in private.
And that kind of purity cannot be manufactured through fear alone.
You cannot shame yourself into loving holiness.
You cannot build lasting transformation merely by hating yourself whenever you fail.
You cannot overcome the deepest disorder of the heart simply by learning to look religious.
The Gospel calls us to something deeper.
To repentance.
To faith.
To abiding in Christ.
To the renewing work of the Holy Spirit.
Galatians 5:16 says:
"Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh."
And Galatians 5:22–23 includes self-control among the fruit of the Spirit.
This is not a promise that Christians will never experience temptation.
It is a call to live under the Spirit's transforming influence rather than surrendering to sinful desires.
Growth may involve difficult decisions.
Repeated resistance.
Honest confession.
New habits.
Patient restoration.
And learning to turn toward Christ before temptation has been allowed to settle in.
You may still have battles.
You may still need help.
You may still experience moments when your old desires seem louder than your new convictions.
But there is a profound difference between struggling against sin and peacefully making a home for it.
The Christian life is not defined by pretending that the battle does not exist.
It is marked by returning to Christ, trusting His grace, and learning to obey Him.
And perhaps one of the most powerful prayers you can pray is not a dramatic speech.
Perhaps it is simply this:
"Jesus, I don't want to keep loving what is destroying my obedience to You. Teach my heart to love what You love."
That prayer may be spoken through tears.
It may be whispered after another failure.
It may be prayed by someone who has no idea how to begin changing.
But it is a prayer directed toward the right Savior.
Because Jesus did not come merely to produce people who are better at hiding their sins.
He came to save sinners.
Matthew 1:21 declares that He would save His people from their sins.
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from public consequences.
From their sins.
And the cross reveals just how seriously God takes both sin and redemption.
Jesus did not die because our sins were insignificant.
He died because our need for salvation was real.
The One who taught about purity of heart lived without sin.
The One who exposed human unrighteousness willingly went to the cross for sinners.
The One who called people to repentance rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who turn to God in faith.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to moral improvement.
The Gospel is not merely, "Stop looking at things you shouldn't look at."
It is the good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again, and that through Him sinners can be reconciled to God.
And reconciliation changes what we live for.
We begin to desire holiness not as a way to purchase God's love, but as the fruit of belonging to Christ.
We learn to resist sin not because we think we can earn salvation, but because the Savior who redeemed us is worthy of our obedience.
We begin to see other people differently.
We begin to see ourselves differently.
And slowly, sometimes painfully, the things we once excused become things we are willing to surrender.
Not because we are trying to impress a watching world.
But because we have encountered a Savior who knows us completely and calls us to walk in His light.
And there is one more thing.
If you have been reading this article while thinking about someone else's sin, be careful.
It is easy to read Matthew 5 and immediately remember the failures of another person.
The unfaithful spouse.
The hypocritical church leader.
The friend who fell into scandal.
The person whose secret became public.
But Jesus' words are not merely ammunition for condemning others.
They are a mirror.
Before you use this passage to expose another person's heart, allow the Lord to examine your own.
Psalm 139:23–24 expresses a prayer every believer needs:
"Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!"
That is a courageous prayer.
Because it asks God to reveal what we would rather conceal.
And perhaps that is what you need tonight.
Not another excuse.
Not another secret promise.
Not another performance of spiritual strength.
But an honest conversation with Jesus.
"Lord, You know."
"You know what I keep returning to."
"You know what I have hidden."
"You know what I have justified."
"You know the people I have hurt."
"You know the desires I have been feeding."
"And You know that I cannot make myself righteous."
"Please forgive me."
"Please change me."
"Teach me to walk in the light."
"Give me the courage to seek help where I need it."
"Teach me to see people the way You want me to see them."
"And let my private life increasingly reflect the faith I profess in public."
There is no need to perform for God.
He already knows the truth.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not to hide from that truth, but to bring it into the light of His mercy.

You do not have to disclose private details or publicly confess anything that would harm you or another person. But if you want to take a small, honest step toward seeking prayer, those three words can be a beginning.
And if you have experienced the patience of Christ through a difficult season of repentance and growth, consider commenting "Christ is still healing me."
Someone reading your words may need to know that the Christian life is not a story of flawless people pretending they have never fallen.
It is a story of sinners learning to depend on a faithful Savior.
Perhaps you know someone who needs to read this.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Not because you want to expose their secrets.
But because they have been struggling with shame and need to hear both the seriousness of sin and the hope of the Gospel.
Not because reading it once will magically remove temptation.
But because there may come a night when you need to remember what Jesus actually said, what He did not say, and why His call to holiness is inseparable from His grace.
Our desire is not merely to produce content that people read and forget.
It is to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through biblical teaching, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the life-changing truth of the Gospel.
These resources are part of our commitment to making Christian teaching and spiritual nourishment accessible.
You can glorify God through obedience, prayer, service, generosity, love, and faithfulness in countless ways.
But if you believe in the mission of this ministry and have the means to support it, your monthly contribution can be one meaningful way of participating in that mission.
It can help us keep reaching people who are struggling, searching, repenting, learning, and discovering the grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the goal has never been merely to grow a page.
The goal is to proclaim Christ.
To teach Scripture faithfully.
To encourage repentance without crushing the repentant.
To speak about holiness without pretending that Christians never struggle.
To make room for honest testimonies of grace.
And to remind people that even the most painful chapters of a life do not have to be its final chapters.
Now, before you leave, return to the question that brought you here.
Why did Jesus say that looking with lust is adultery of the heart?
Because He knows that sin is not merely a matter of what we do when people are watching.
It is also a matter of what we choose to cherish when nobody else can see.
Because faithfulness is more than avoiding physical betrayal.
Because people are made for dignity, not exploitation.
Because God's commandments reveal a holiness that reaches beyond appearances.
And because Jesus loves us enough to confront the things we are tempted to excuse.
But please do not walk away remembering only the confrontation.
Remember the Savior.
Remember that He knows the heart.
Remember that He calls sinners to repentance.
Remember that His death and resurrection are the foundation of our hope.
Remember that forgiveness is available through Him.
Remember that transformation is possible through the grace of God and the work of His Spirit.
And remember that your secret struggle, however serious, does not have to be the end of your story.
If you are living in sin, do not make peace with it.
If you are trapped in shame, do not mistake shame for repentance.
If you have hurt someone, do not use grace as an excuse to avoid responsibility.
If you need help, seek it.
If you need to confess, bring the truth into the light with wisdom and appropriate accountability.
If you have fallen, turn again to Christ.
And if you are standing today, remain humble and watchful, knowing that your strength is never independent of God's grace.
The Jesus who said, "You have already committed adultery in your heart," is the same Jesus who gave His life to save sinners.
That is not a contradiction.
That is the breathtaking truth of the Gospel.
His holiness exposes us.
His mercy invites us.
His cross offers forgiveness.
His resurrection announces victory.
And His Spirit calls us into a new way of living.

So tonight, when the room becomes quiet, when the screen is within reach, when temptation whispers that nobody will ever know, remember that your next decision is not merely about whether you will be caught.
It is about the kind of person you are becoming before God.
And when you feel the weight of your past, remember this as well:
You do not have to spend the rest of your life pretending that the old story is all there is.
Come to Jesus.
Bring Him the truth.
Turn from sin.
Trust His grace.
And follow Him into the light.
Because the heart that once became a hiding place for sin can, by the grace of Jesus Christ, become a living testimony that redemption has the final word.
